threads.Author: claude
threads.Text: Unverified assumption, stated as one. I confirmed _meta.systemPrompt works with claude-agent-acp because I watched it in the trace. I have NOT confirmed codex-acp honours it — that is inference from both implementing ACP, which is exactly the reasoning the research doc warns against, since _meta semantics are explicitly not standardised. This is the single cheapest thing to check before phase 4: one session/new against codex-acp and read the system prompt back.

threads.Author: claude
threads.Text: I want to flag the bypassPermissions line as load-bearing and slightly uncomfortable. It is literally true that the permission layer is already off, so owning tools is not a regression on paper. But it is the kind of true-and-convenient argument that deserves scrutiny: Claude Code still applies its own internal guards and refusals even under bypassPermissions, and a native loop would not inherit those for free. I would not lean on this line as reassurance.

threads.Author: claude
threads.Text: The scope here is genuinely uncertain and I would not trust my own estimate. 'Owns the loop' hides a lot: retry semantics, partial tool failures, streaming interruption mid-tool-call, context-window overflow handling, prompt caching. Claude Code does all of this today and we have never had to think about it. MCP covers tool TRANSPORT, not tool SEMANTICS — a Bash tool that hangs, or an Edit that half-applies, is ours to get right. Before committing to phase 5 I would want a spike: one tool-calling turn, end to end, timeboxed, to replace this paragraph with a real number.

threads.Author: claude
threads.Text: This is the judgement call I would most expect you to push back on, and you would have a case. Phase 4 builds a runtime you do not especially want (Codex) purely to stress-test the interface. The argument for it is that an adapter reveals interface mistakes in days where a half-written loop reveals them in weeks — but that is my estimate, not a measurement. If you would rather go straight from 3 to 5, the honest risk is that you discover the abstraction is wrong while also debugging tool execution, and cannot tell which is at fault.

threads.Author: claude
threads.Text: Why measurement is phase 1 and not a success criterion at the end: today's drain-barrier bug and yesterday's absorb race were both found in production, after the fact, by someone noticing behaviour. Nothing in this repo has ever predicted a latency regression. If phase 5 lands and turns feel slower, without this we would be arguing from memory. Cheap to do, and it is the only phase that produces evidence rather than code.

threads.Author: claude
threads.Text: The fence I care most about. Every previous attempt in this repo to touch the turn path while doing something else went badly — the queue cutover produced the dead drain barrier, and the absorb fix produced a late-answered turn. The 429 lines are where quality lives and they are not on the critical path for any of this. If a phase seems to need a change there, that is a signal the phase is wrong, not that the fence is.
